questions.q: Why is the ApplianceMakers Warranty Network integration built as an outbound Apex callout rather than an inbound REST endpoint?
options: Because Salesforce cannot expose inbound REST endpoints
Because inbound integrations require a different programming language
Because Salesforce is the caller and the manufacturer's system is the callee -- Salesforce initiates the request
Because outbound callouts don't require any authentication
questions.explain: This is an outbound integration: Solstice's org calls out to the manufacturer's API, making it an Apex HTTP callout rather than an exposed inbound endpoint.

questions.q: Why does `req.setEndpoint()` use `callout:ApplianceMakers_Warranty/claims` instead of a literal URL?
options: The callout: prefix is required syntax for routing the request through a Named Credential, keeping the real URL and auth secret out of the Apex code
It's just a stylistic preference with no functional effect
Literal URLs are not supported by the Http class
It makes the callout run synchronously instead of asynchronously
questions.explain: The callout:Name syntax routes the request through a Named Credential, which is how the real endpoint URL and authentication secret are kept out of the Apex source code.

questions.q: What does `JSON.deserializeUntyped()` return, as used in `submitClaim`?
options: A strongly-typed Apex wrapper class instance
An untyped Map<String, Object> / List<Object> structure that must be cast field by field
A raw HttpResponse object
Nothing -- it is a void method
questions.explain: JSON.deserializeUntyped() returns an untyped Map/List structure, appropriate for this small, simple response rather than defining a full typed wrapper class.

questions.q: Why does `submitClaim` explicitly check `res.getStatusCode()` instead of relying on a thrown exception to detect failure?
options: Because Apex callouts always throw an exception on any non-200 status, making the check redundant
Because getStatusCode() is required syntax with no functional purpose
Because exceptions cannot be thrown from Queueable context
Because http.send() does not throw an exception for a 4xx or 5xx HTTP status -- a response describing failure is still a successful callout from Apex's point of view
questions.explain: A callout that receives a 400 or 500 response doesn't throw an Apex exception on its own -- the code must check the status code itself and raise its own exception when the call wasn't actually successful.

questions.q: Why is `WarrantyClaimSubmissionQueueable` (from Lesson 11) allowed to call `ManufacturerWarrantyClient.submitClaim()`?
options: Because that Queueable implements Database.AllowsCallouts, which is required for a class to legally make an HTTP callout from async context
Because all Apex classes can make callouts by default
Because the method name starts with 'submit'
Because Warranty_Claim__c has a special callout permission field
questions.explain: Only a class that implements Database.AllowsCallouts (or runs outside restricted contexts like a trigger) may make HTTP callouts -- that Queueable already declared it in Lesson 11, which is what makes this callout legal.
